text:
Sampled HR@10 can misrepresent full-catalog ranking and even reverse model comparisons; repeating 99-negative draws reduces sampling variability but does not remove systematic bias. [Krichene and Rendle](https://research.google/pubs/on-sampled-metrics-for-item-recommendation/) establish this inconsistency. [RecSys 2025 research](https://doi.org/10.1145/3705328.3748086) examines sampling reliability through resolution, fidelity, robustness and recovery of ground-truth model rankings, reporting 95% bootstrap intervals. [Subbiah et al., 2024](https://arxiv.org/abs/2410.06371) develop corrected rank estimates for sampled WARP/LambdaRank training; these are relevant methodological leads, rather than evidence that corrected sampled HR@10 reliably recovers full-catalog performance.

Popularity stratification matters: [Prakash et al., 2024](https://arxiv.org/abs/2410.17276) show that aggregate sequential-recommendation metrics conceal head/mid/tail differences, with negative-sampling choices affecting these groups differently. Practical diagnostic proposal: use public training-prefix targets, define frequency bands using training interactions only, cross-tabulate by history length, and compare repeated uniform candidate sets with popularity-stratified difficulty probes. Reuse identical users, targets and candidate draws across diagnostic comparisons; bootstrap paired user-level differences within categories, then macro-average, reporting candidate-draw variability separately. Treat popularity-sampled results as a different diagnostic task unless appropriately weighted. For the twenty designated users, score unseen catalogs in chunks to obtain exact prefix-target ranks and recommendation popularity profiles; compare these with sampled diagnostics. This protocol is a synthesis, not an established guarantee: twenty users provide a limited case study, and unseen items are not confirmed dislikes. Keep the host’s pinned validation evaluator and single BERT4Rec checkpoint per category unchanged.
